contrast: Informal and mild, often affectionate. *Drive someone batty* means 'annoy someone a lot'.

senses.gloss: Slightly crazy or strange in a harmless way.
examples: My *batty* old aunt still talks to her plants.
That constant beeping is driving me *batty*.
His ideas got *battier* every year.

senses.gloss: Of or from Bavaria, a state in southern Germany.
examples: We ate at a *Bavarian* restaurant in Chicago.
The *Bavarian* Alps are beautiful in winter.
Her grandparents were *Bavarian*.

senses.gloss: Funny in a rude way about sex.
examples: The comedian told a few *bawdy* jokes.
The play is pretty *bawdy* for a high school audience.
The sailors sang the *bawdiest* songs they knew.

senses.gloss: Decorated with small beads.
examples: She wore a *beaded* dress to the wedding.
Her moccasins are *beaded* and fringed.

senses.gloss: Covered with small drops of liquid.
examples: His forehead was *beaded* with sweat.
The cold glass was *beaded* with water.

senses.gloss: (Of eyes) small, round and shiny, often in a way that seems unfriendly or greedy.
examples: The crow watched us with its *beady* black eyes.
I don't trust that guy with the *beady* little eyes.
The villain had the *beadiest* eyes in the whole cartoon.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb *beam*: *She was beaming*

senses.gloss: Smiling widely because very happy.
examples: The *beaming* parents posed with their son at graduation.
She walked in with a *beaming* smile.
The *beaming* winner held up the trophy.

senses.gloss: Possible to accept or deal with, though unpleasant.
examples: The heat was *bearable* once the sun went down.
A good book makes a long flight more *bearable*.
The pain was barely *bearable*.

senses.gloss: Having a beard.
examples: A *bearded* man in a flannel shirt answered the door.
Half the guys in the band are *bearded*.
He's been *bearded* since college.

form: -ish from *bear* (a trader who expects prices to fall)

senses.gloss: Expecting prices on a financial market to fall.
examples: Many analysts are *bearish* on oil right now.
The market has been *bearish* for months.
Investors grew more *bearish* after the jobs report.

senses.gloss: Big, heavy and a little rough, like a bear.
examples: He gave me a *bearish* hug.
Her dad is a *bearish* guy with a surprisingly soft voice.

position: predicative only — never before a noun: *a tired worker*, not *a beat worker*
comparison: not gradable — an extreme word like *exhausted*: *totally beat*
contrast: *I'm beat* is not the past tense of the verb; it means 'I'm exhausted'. The participle of the verb is *beaten*: *a beaten team*.

senses.gloss: Very tired.
examples: I'm *beat* — I'm going to bed.
After the double shift she was totally *beat*.
You look *beat*. Sit down for a minute.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *beat up* or *beat-up* after a verb
contrast: *Beat someone up* is the phrasal verb 'hit someone many times'. The adjective is about things worn out by use.

senses.gloss: Old and in bad condition from a lot of use.
examples: He drives a *beat-up* old pickup.
My sneakers are pretty *beat-up*.
This couch is even more *beat-up* than the last one.

contrast: *Off the beaten path* is the usual American form; British English says *off the beaten track*.

senses.gloss: Defeated, and feeling that you have lost.
examples: The *beaten* team walked slowly off the field.
After the third rejection he felt *beaten*.

senses.gloss: (Of a path) worn flat by many people walking on it.
examples: We followed a *beaten* path through the woods.
The best restaurants are off the *beaten* path.

senses.gloss: (Of eggs or cream) mixed quickly until smooth.
examples: Add two *beaten* eggs to the flour.
Brush the dough with *beaten* egg before baking.

contrast: Russian *красивый* works for men too, but English usually calls a man *handsome* or *good-looking*; *a beautiful man* sounds poetic. Never *beautifuller*.

senses.gloss: Very attractive to look at.
examples: She has a *beautiful* smile.
The view from the top is *beautiful*.
It's the most *beautiful* beach I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Very pleasant or good; done very well.
examples: What a *beautiful* day!
That was a *beautiful* pass.
She's a *beautiful* person, inside and out.

contrast: Old-fashioned. Everyday English says *That color looks good on you* or *suits you*. The negative is more common, as in *conduct unbecoming an officer*.

senses.gloss: (Of clothes or a hairstyle) making someone look attractive.
examples: She wore a *becoming* shade of blue.
The short haircut is very *becoming*.
I think the green dress is more *becoming* than the red one.

senses.gloss: Wet, dirty and messy.
examples: A *bedraggled* cat showed up at our door in the rain.
The hikers looked *bedraggled* after two days in the storm.
By morning the flowers looked even more *bedraggled*.

senses.gloss: Too sick or weak to get out of bed.
examples: Her grandmother has been *bedridden* for a year.
He takes care of his *bedridden* father.
The flu left me *bedridden* for a week.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the phrasal verb: *Security was beefed up*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *beef up* (make stronger)

senses.gloss: Made bigger, stronger or more effective.
examples: There's *beefed-up* security at the airport this week.
The new model has a *beefed-up* engine.
The *beefed-up* defense held the other team to one goal.

senses.gloss: (Of a person) big, strong and heavy.
examples: Two *beefy* guys carried the piano upstairs.
He got a lot *beefier* after a year at the gym.

senses.gloss: Bigger or more powerful than usual.
examples: The laptop has a *beefy* processor.
You'll need a *beefier* battery for that drill.

position: after the noun — with its own object: *a welcome befitting a hero*
takes: a noun directly, with no preposition: *befitting a queen*
contrast: Everyday English prefers *fitting* or *suitable* (*a fitting tribute*). The verb is common too: *as befits a champion*.

senses.gloss: Suitable for a particular person or occasion.
examples: They gave him a funeral *befitting* a president.
She dressed in a style *befitting* her new job.
The team celebrated in a manner *befitting* champions.

senses.gloss: Confused and unable to think clearly.
examples: A *befuddled* tourist asked us for directions.
I was completely *befuddled* by the new tax forms.
The more he explained, the more *befuddled* we got.

contrast: *A beginning student* is American; British English prefers *a beginner* or *a beginners' class*. *The beginning* on its own is the noun.

senses.gloss: At the first level; for people just starting to learn something.
examples: She teaches *beginning* Spanish at the community college.
This series is for *beginning* readers.
The class is full of *beginning* guitar players.

senses.gloss: Charming and attractive, sometimes in a way that misleads.
examples: She had a *beguiling* smile.
The idea is *beguiling*, but it won't work in practice.
It's one of the most *beguiling* novels of the year.

contrast: American spelling; British English writes *behavioural*.

senses.gloss: Connected with how people or animals behave.
examples: The school hired a *behavioral* specialist.
*Behavioral* therapy helped him with his anxiety.
Scientists studied *behavioral* changes in the mice.

position: attributive only — after a verb it has no hyphens: *work behind the scenes*

senses.gloss: Happening in private, out of public view.
examples: The DVD includes a *behind-the-scenes* look at the movie.
There was a lot of *behind-the-scenes* negotiating before the deal.
Her *behind-the-scenes* work kept the campaign running.

senses.gloss: Owing something to someone, so that you must do what they want.
examples: The senator is *beholden* to big donors.
I don't want to be *beholden* to anyone.
Local papers were *beholden* to their advertisers.

contrast: The older spelling *Byelorussian* is dated. Also a noun for the person and the language.

senses.gloss: Of or from Belarus, its people or its language.
examples: She's a *Belarusian* tennis player.
*Belarusian* and Russian are both official languages there.
His parents are *Belarusian*.

senses.gloss: Coming or happening later than it should.
examples: Happy *belated* birthday!
I sent her a *belated* thank-you note.
His apology was sincere but *belated*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Belgium.
examples: We had *Belgian* waffles for breakfast.
Is this chocolate *Belgian*?
The *Belgian* rider won the race.

contrast: In everyday talk *unbelievable* usually means 'amazing' (*The game was unbelievable!*); *believable* only means 'realistic, easy to believe'.

senses.gloss: Easy to believe; seeming real.
examples: The characters in the show are very *believable*.
He needed a *believable* excuse for being late.
Her second version of the story was more *believable*.

senses.gloss: Making someone or something seem unimportant.
examples: Her boss made *belittling* comments about her work.
His tone was *belittling*.
It was the most *belittling* thing anyone had ever said to me.

senses.gloss: (Of pants) very wide at the bottom of the legs.
examples: She found a pair of *bell-bottom* jeans at a thrift store.
*Bell-bottom* pants were everywhere in the 1970s.
The sailors wore white *bell-bottom* trousers.

senses.gloss: Shaped like a bell, narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.
examples: Test scores usually fall on a *bell-shaped* curve.
The plant has small *bell-shaped* flowers.
The lampshade is *bell-shaped*.

senses.gloss: Eager to fight or start a war.
examples: The general's *bellicose* speech worried the neighboring countries.
The president's tone has become more *bellicose*.
He gets *bellicose* when he drinks.

senses.gloss: Angry and ready to argue or fight.
examples: The *belligerent* customer was asked to leave.
He got *belligerent* when the police arrived.
Her emails grew more *belligerent* every week.

senses.gloss: (Formal, of a country or group) fighting in a war.
examples: The *belligerent* nations agreed to a ceasefire.
Neither of the *belligerent* sides would give up the city.

form: compound — *belly* + *up*, like a dead fish floating upside down

senses.gloss: (Of a business) failed or bankrupt.
examples: The restaurant went *belly-up* after a year.
Half the startups in that building have gone *belly-up*.
If sales don't improve, we'll be *belly-up* by summer.

senses.gloss: Loved very much.
examples: He was a *beloved* teacher at the school for thirty years.
The park is *beloved* by locals.
She's one of the most *beloved* singers in the country.

position: both — *That was below the belt*; hyphenated before a noun: *a below-the-belt joke*
comparison: not gradable — though *a little below the belt* is common
form: idiom — from boxing, where hitting below the belt is against the rules

senses.gloss: Unfair and hurtful.
examples: That comment about his divorce was *below the belt*.
Bringing up her weight was a little *below the belt*.
The ad was a *below-the-belt* attack on his family.

contrast: A trap: *bemused* traditionally means 'puzzled', not 'amused'. Many Americans now use it for 'mildly amused', so context decides; careful writers keep it for 'puzzled'.

senses.gloss: Puzzled and a little confused.
examples: He looked *bemused* by all the questions.
She gave me a *bemused* look when I answered in French.

senses.gloss: Mildly amused, often because something seems odd.
examples: He watched the kids' argument with a *bemused* smile.
She read the angry comments with *bemused* detachment.

senses.gloss: Easy to bend without breaking.
examples: The toy has *bendable* arms and legs.
Give the kids *bendable* straws.
This wire is more *bendable* than the old kind.

senses.gloss: Having a good effect; helpful.
examples: Regular exercise is *beneficial* to your health.
The deal was *beneficial* for both companies.
Some bacteria are actually *beneficial*.

senses.gloss: Kind and wanting to help others.
examples: He ran the company like a *benevolent* grandfather.
The old king was seen as *benevolent*.

senses.gloss: (Of an organization) set up to help people in need.
examples: The *benevolent* society paid for the funeral.
He left his money to a police *benevolent* association.

contrast: Covers both Bangladesh and the Indian state of West Bengal. Also the name of the language and a person: *She speaks Bengali*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Bengal, its people or its language.
examples: We ordered *Bengali* fish curry.
*Bengali* literature has a long history.
Her family is *Bengali*.

comparison: more/most — not gradable in the medical sense
contrast: The *g* is silent: it rhymes with *nine*.

senses.gloss: (Of a tumor or growth) not cancerous.
examples: Luckily, the tumor was *benign*.
The doctor removed a small *benign* growth.

senses.gloss: Not harmful or dangerous.
examples: Most of these apps are fairly *benign*.
The side effects are usually *benign*.

senses.gloss: Kind, gentle or mild.
examples: He had a *benign* smile.
The weather was *benign* all week.

contrast: *Bent on* something means 'determined to do it' — see *bent on*. British slang *bent* 'dishonest' is not used in American English.

senses.gloss: No longer straight; curved or folded.
examples: The nail was *bent*, so I pulled it out.
Keep your knees *bent* when you lift the box.
The front wheel of my bike is *bent*.

senses.gloss: (Of a person) bending forward.
examples: An old man, *bent* with age, shuffled past.
She sat *bent* over her desk all afternoon.

senses.gloss: (bent out of shape, informal) Upset or angry.
examples: Don't get all *bent* out of shape about it.
He got *bent* out of shape over a parking ticket.

position: predicative only — also directly after a noun: *a man bent on revenge*
comparison: not gradable — *hell-bent on* is the strong form

senses.gloss: Determined to do something, often something bad.
examples: He seems *bent on* ruining my weekend.
The team came out *bent on* revenge.
She's *bent on* becoming a pilot.

contrast: *The bereaved* is used as a noun for the people whose relative has died. Compare *bereft*, which is about a feeling of loss or lack.

senses.gloss: Having lost a close relative or friend who has died.
examples: The *bereaved* family asked for privacy.
Counselors are available for *bereaved* parents.
She was recently *bereaved* and still in shock.

position: predicative only — *a bereft mother* is rare

senses.gloss: Completely without something.
examples: The team seemed *bereft* of ideas.
The town was *bereft* of jobs after the plant closed.

senses.gloss: Very sad and lonely because someone has died or left.
examples: She was *bereft* after her husband died.
The kids felt *bereft* when their best friend moved away.

senses.gloss: Wildly out of control, with anger or excitement.
examples: The crowd went *berserk* when the band came on.
The dog goes *berserk* whenever the mail carrier comes.
My phone went *berserk* and started calling people.

senses.gloss: Surrounded by an army that is trying to capture it.
examples: Food was running out in the *besieged* city.
The *besieged* soldiers held out for six months.

senses.gloss: Overwhelmed by many people, questions or requests.
examples: The *besieged* star hid from photographers.
Teachers say they feel *besieged* by new rules.

senses.gloss: So in love with someone or something that you cannot think clearly.
examples: He's completely *besotted* with his new girlfriend.
The *besotted* grandparents took hundreds of photos.
She's *besotted* with that puppy.

senses.gloss: Wearing glasses.
examples: A *bespectacled* librarian helped us find the book.
The suspect was described as tall and *bespectacled*.
The *bespectacled* professor peered over his notes.

contrast: Originally British. Americans usually say *custom* or *custom-made*; *bespoke* sounds upscale and shows up in marketing (*bespoke software*, *bespoke cocktails*).

senses.gloss: Made specially for one customer.
examples: He paid $5,000 for a *bespoke* suit.
The agency builds *bespoke* software for banks.
Every piece of furniture in the hotel is *bespoke*.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *best known* after a verb

senses.gloss: Known by the most people.
examples: It's her *best-known* novel.
He's *best known* for his role in a TV comedy.
The *best-known* landmark in the city is the bridge.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *best loved* after a verb

senses.gloss: Loved by the most people.
examples: It's one of America's *best-loved* songs.
The bakery's *best-loved* item is the cinnamon roll.
Of all his books, this one is *best loved* by kids.

comparison: not gradable — *best* is already built in
contrast: *A best-selling author* usually just means 'very popular, on the bestseller list', not literally number one.

senses.gloss: Selling in very large numbers.
examples: She's a *best-selling* author with over twenty novels.
It was the *best-selling* car in America last year.
The album became their *best-selling* record.

position: both — mostly after a verb; hyphenated before a noun: *better-off families*
comparison: irregular — the comparative of *well off*: *well off*, *better off*, *best off*
contrast: *You'd be better off* + *-ing* is a common way to give advice: *You'd be better off calling first*.

senses.gloss: In a better situation.
examples: You'd be *better off* taking the train.
She's *better off* without him.
We'd have been *best off* staying home.

senses.gloss: Having more money.
examples: Most families are *better off* than they were ten years ago.
The *better-off* neighborhoods are on the north side.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *better known* after a verb
contrast: *Better known as* introduces the more familiar name: *Samuel Clemens, better known as Mark Twain*.

senses.gloss: Known by more people.
examples: He's *better known* as a singer than as an actor.
The *better-known* brands cost twice as much.
Samuel Clemens, *better known* as Mark Twain, grew up in Missouri.

senses.gloss: More attractive to look at.
examples: He's much *better-looking* in person.
The new phone is *better-looking* than the old one.
She married the *best-looking* guy in her class.

contrast: *Bewildered* is how you feel; *bewildering* is what causes the feeling: *a bewildering choice of cereals*.

senses.gloss: Very confused and not sure what to do.
examples: A *bewildered* tourist stood in the middle of the station.
I was *bewildered* by all the forms.
She looked even more *bewildered* after his explanation.

comparison: more/most — not gradable in the magic sense

senses.gloss: Under a magic spell.
examples: In the story, the prince lives in a *bewitched* castle.
The villagers believed the well was *bewitched*.

senses.gloss: Strongly attracted or charmed.
examples: He was completely *bewitched* by her voice.
*Bewitched* audiences stayed until the last song.

senses.gloss: So beautiful or charming that you cannot stop looking or listening.
examples: She had *bewitching* green eyes.
The music was strange and *bewitching*.
It's the most *bewitching* place I've ever visited.

contrast: Also an adverb phrase after verbs: *proved beyond doubt*. The American legal standard is *beyond a reasonable doubt*.

senses.gloss: Certain; impossible to question.
examples: Her talent is *beyond doubt*.
The facts of the case are now *beyond doubt*.
His loyalty to the team was never *beyond doubt*.

senses.gloss: Of or from Bhutan.
examples: *Bhutanese* food is famous for its chili peppers.
The *Bhutanese* government measures 'Gross National Happiness'.
Many families in the neighborhood are *Bhutanese*.

contrast: Easy to confuse with *biennial* (every two years). *Biannual* means twice a year; *twice-yearly* is clearer.

senses.gloss: Happening twice a year.
examples: The store's *biannual* sale is in January and July.
Don't forget your *biannual* dental checkup.
The board holds *biannual* meetings in spring and fall.

senses.gloss: Unfairly favoring one side.
examples: The referee was clearly *biased* against our team.
Many viewers think the coverage is *biased*.
The survey questions were *biased* toward younger people.

senses.gloss: Relating to or found in the Bible.
examples: The movie tells a *biblical* story.
The name Noah is *biblical*.

senses.gloss: Very large or extreme, like events in the Bible.
examples: The city faced a traffic jam of *biblical* proportions.
The flooding this spring was *biblical*.

senses.gloss: Relating to lists of books and articles.
examples: The book ends with a long *bibliographical* note.
Check the *bibliographical* details before you submit the paper.
The library keeps *bibliographical* records for every item.

senses.gloss: (Of a lawmaking body) having two parts, or houses.
examples: The US Congress is a *bicameral* legislature.
Nebraska is the only state whose legislature is not *bicameral*.
Most large democracies have *bicameral* parliaments.

contrast: American English; British English prefers *bicentenary*. Also a noun: *the nation's bicentennial in 1976*.

senses.gloss: Marking two hundred years since something happened.
examples: The town held a *bicentennial* parade.
My parents still have a *bicentennial* quarter from 1976.
The university is planning its *bicentennial* celebration.

ru: проходящий раз в два года; двулетний
contrast: *Biennial* is every two years; *biannual* is twice a year.

senses.gloss: Happening every two years.
examples: The art show is a *biennial* event.
The *biennial* conference will meet again in 2028.

senses.gloss: (Of a plant) living for two years.
examples: Parsley is a *biennial* plant.
*Biennial* flowers bloom only in their second year.

contrast: Often a gentle or joking way to avoid saying 'overweight'.

senses.gloss: Having a large, heavy body frame.
examples: He's a *big-boned* farm kid from Iowa.
I'm not fat, I'm just *big-boned*!
The breed is tall and *big-boned*.

senses.gloss: Expensive.
examples: Families are putting off *big-ticket* purchases like cars.
Refrigerators and TVs are *big-ticket* items.
The *big-ticket* projects were cut from the budget.

senses.gloss: Having strong, unfair opinions about people of another race, religion or group.
examples: He made a *bigoted* comment about immigrants.
Her uncle's views are openly *bigoted*.
It was the most *bigoted* speech I've ever heard.

senses.gloss: Between two countries or groups.
examples: The two countries signed a *bilateral* trade agreement.
*Bilateral* talks will continue next week.

senses.gloss: (Medical) on both sides of the body.
examples: She had *bilateral* knee surgery.
The hearing loss is *bilateral*.

senses.gloss: Speaking two languages well, or using two languages.
examples: Their kids are *bilingual* in English and Spanish.
The school offers *bilingual* classes.
Road signs in the area are *bilingual*.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb *billow*: *smoke was billowing*

senses.gloss: Rising or spreading out in large waves or clouds.
examples: *Billowing* smoke rose from the warehouse.
She wore a white dress with *billowing* sleeves.
We watched the *billowing* storm clouds roll in.

ru: выходящий раз в два месяца; дважды в месяц
contrast: Ambiguous: usually 'every two months', but sometimes 'twice a month'. *Every other month* or *twice a month* (*semimonthly*) is clearer. Also an adverb: *The magazine comes out bimonthly*.

senses.gloss: Happening every two months.
examples: The newsletter is *bimonthly*.
We get a *bimonthly* water bill.

senses.gloss: Happening twice a month.
examples: The club holds *bimonthly* meetings on the first and third Tuesdays.
The *bimonthly* farmers market runs on the 1st and the 15th.

senses.gloss: Using only the digits 0 and 1.
examples: Computers store data in *binary* code.
Write the number 5 in *binary* form.

senses.gloss: Having only two parts or two options.
examples: Life isn't a *binary* choice between success and failure.
Many people reject a *binary* view of gender.

contrast: *The binding* (noun) is the cover and spine of a book, or the part of a ski that holds the boot.

senses.gloss: (Of an agreement or decision) that must be obeyed by law.
examples: The contract is legally *binding*.
The decision is *binding* on both parties.
They signed a *binding* agreement.

senses.gloss: Relating to the chemical processes in living things.
examples: Stress causes *biochemical* changes in the brain.
She works in a *biochemical* research lab.
The test measures *biochemical* markers in the blood.

senses.gloss: Able to break down naturally and not harm the environment.
examples: The cups are made of *biodegradable* plastic.
Is this packaging *biodegradable*?
Paper bags are *biodegradable*, but they still take energy to make.

senses.gloss: About the facts of a person's life.
examples: The movie is a *biographical* drama about a jazz singer.
The website has a short *biographical* note on each author.
Please include some *biographical* information with your application.

contrast: For parents, *biological* is the neutral word; *real mother* can hurt adoptive families. Russian *родной* is wider: *родной язык* is *native language*, not *biological*.

senses.gloss: Relating to living things or to biology.
examples: Sleep is a basic *biological* need.
The causes of the disease are partly *biological*.

senses.gloss: Related by birth, not by adoption or marriage.
examples: She found her *biological* mother at age thirty.
He's not my *biological* dad, but he raised me.

senses.gloss: (Of weapons) using germs to cause disease.
examples: The treaty bans *biological* weapons.
Officials trained for a possible *biological* attack.

senses.gloss: Relating to both biology and medicine.
examples: He studied *biomedical* engineering.
The company makes *biomedical* devices like pacemakers.
The grant funds *biomedical* research on cancer.

senses.gloss: Having or being electronic body parts.
examples: The veteran walks on a *bionic* leg.
Researchers are testing a *bionic* eye.

senses.gloss: (Informal) Stronger or better than a normal person.
examples: Our goalie has *bionic* reflexes.
She must have *bionic* hearing — she heard us from upstairs.

contrast: A key word in US politics: supported by both Democrats and Republicans.

senses.gloss: Supported by or involving both main political parties.
examples: The bill passed with *bipartisan* support.
A *bipartisan* group of senators wrote the plan.
Voters want a more *bipartisan* approach.

contrast: Using *bipolar* casually for 'moody' (*the weather is so bipolar*) is common but offends many people.

senses.gloss: Having bipolar disorder, a mental illness with extreme changes of mood.
examples: Her brother was diagnosed with *bipolar* disorder.
He's *bipolar* and takes medication for it.

senses.gloss: Having two opposite poles or two main powers.
examples: The *bipolar* world of the Cold War ended in 1991.
Scientists studied the star's *bipolar* jets of gas.

senses.gloss: Having parents of two different races.
senses.ru: с родителями разных рас, смешанного происхождения
examples: She's *biracial* — her mom is Korean and her dad is Black.
The show follows a *biracial* family in Atlanta.
Many *biracial* Americans check more than one box on the census.

contrast: Also a noun (*a bisexual*), but the adjective is more usual; *bi* is the informal short form.

senses.gloss: Sexually attracted to more than one gender.
examples: He came out as *bisexual* in college.
The novel has a *bisexual* main character.
The group supports gay, lesbian and *bisexual* teens.

contrast: Rude slang, mostly about women; avoid it in polite or professional speech.

senses.gloss: Mean and unkind in what you say about people.
examples: She made a *bitchy* remark about my hair.
Sorry I was so *bitchy* this morning.
The comments got *bitchier* as the night went on.

senses.gloss: (Of wind or cold) so cold that it hurts.
examples: We walked home in the *biting* wind.
The cold that morning was *biting*.

senses.gloss: (Of words) sharp and cruel.
examples: The critic wrote a *biting* review.
Her humor is more *biting* than her sister's.

contrast: Russian *горький перец* is *hot pepper* in English: *bitter* is the taste of coffee, dark chocolate or medicine, never spicy heat.

senses.gloss: Having a strong, sharp taste that is not sweet.
examples: This coffee is too *bitter* for me.
The longer the tea steeps, the *more bitter* it gets.

senses.gloss: Angry and upset because you think you were treated unfairly.
examples: He's still *bitter* about losing his job.
She gave a short, *bitter* laugh.

senses.gloss: Making you very unhappy; hard to accept.
examples: The loss was a *bitter* disappointment.
She learned from *bitter* experience not to trust him.

senses.gloss: Full of hate; very intense.
examples: The two brothers became *bitter* enemies.
It was the *bitterest* election fight in years.

senses.gloss: (Of weather) extremely cold.
examples: A *bitter* wind blew off the lake.
Chicago had its *bitterest* winter in decades.

contrast: In American recipes *bittersweet chocolate* is dark chocolate with only a little sugar.

senses.gloss: Happy and sad at the same time.
examples: Graduation was a *bittersweet* day for her.
The ending of the movie is *bittersweet*.

senses.gloss: (Of chocolate) dark and only slightly sweet.
examples: Melt six ounces of *bittersweet* chocolate.
I prefer *bittersweet* chocolate to milk chocolate.

ru: раз в две недели; дважды в неделю
contrast: Ambiguous: in the US it usually means 'every two weeks' (*a biweekly paycheck*), but it can mean 'twice a week'. *Every other week* or *twice a week* is clearer. Also an adverb: *We get paid biweekly*.

senses.gloss: Happening every two weeks.
examples: Most of us get a *biweekly* paycheck.
The team has *biweekly* planning meetings.

senses.gloss: Happening twice a week.
examples: She has *biweekly* physical therapy, on Tuesdays and Fridays.
The paper went from weekly to *biweekly* delivery, Mondays and Thursdays.

contrast: Sounds almost like *bazaar* (a market), but means 'very strange'.

senses.gloss: Very strange and unusual.
examples: I had a *bizarre* dream last night.
His behavior at the party was *bizarre*.
It's the most *bizarre* story I've heard all year.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *black and blue* after a verb

senses.gloss: Covered in bruises.
examples: His arm was *black and blue* after the fall.
She showed me her *black-and-blue* knee.
The older kids beat him *black and blue*.

position: both — hyphenated before a noun; *black and white* after a verb
comparison: not gradable — but in the second sense *as*, *so*, *very* are common: *not as black and white as it looks*
contrast: *In black and white* (a noun phrase) means 'in writing': *It's right there in black and white*.

senses.gloss: Showing only black, white and gray, with no other colors.
examples: Grandpa watched *black-and-white* TV as a kid.
The old photos are all *black and white*.

senses.gloss: Seeing things as simply right or wrong, with nothing in between.
examples: Life isn't as *black and white* as you think.
He has a very *black-and-white* view of the world.

form: compound — *black* + *tie* (a bow tie worn with a tuxedo)
contrast: *Black-tie* means men wear a tuxedo; *white-tie* is even more formal. On invitations the dress code is written without a hyphen: *Black tie optional*.

senses.gloss: Requiring formal evening clothes.
examples: They're going to a *black-tie* dinner at the museum.
The gala is *black-tie*, so rent a tux.
Is the wedding *black-tie* or casual?
